lesson.title: Two Sides of the Same Electron: Redox Reactions
lesson.summary: A redox reaction is any reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur together, since the electrons one species loses are exactly the electrons another species gains.
lesson.body:
Redox is a portmanteau of reduction and oxidation, and the name is chosen deliberately: you cannot have one without the other. If some species in a reaction loses electrons, as you learned oxidation requires, those electrons have to land somewhere, and wherever they land, that species has, by definition, gained electrons and been reduced. Oxidation and reduction are two views of the exact same event, electrons moving from one place to another. A redox reaction is simply any reaction where this electron movement happens, which you can detect by checking whether any atom's oxidation number changes at all.

The magnesium and oxygen example from the last two chapters is a complete redox reaction when you write it as a whole: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) is right arrow 2MgO(s). Check the atom balance first: 2 magnesium atoms on each side, and 2 oxygen atoms on each side, one from O2 and one in each of the two MgO formula units. The equation is balanced. Now check oxidation numbers: magnesium goes from 0 to +2, an increase, so it is oxidized. Oxygen goes from 0 to -2, a decrease, so it is reduced. Both changes are present in the same equation, which is exactly what makes this a redox reaction.

Redox reactions are not limited to metals burning in air. Here is a second example you can actually watch happen in a beaker: drop a strip of zinc metal into a blue solution of copper sulfate. Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) is right arrow Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s). Check the atoms: 1 zinc atom and 1 copper atom on each side. Check the charge, which matters just as much as atoms once ions are involved: the left side has neutral zinc, charge 0, plus Cu2+, charge +2, for a total of +2. The right side has Zn2+, charge +2, plus neutral copper metal, charge 0, also totaling +2. Both sides carry a net charge of +2, so the equation is balanced. Watch the reaction and you will see reddish copper metal plate out onto the zinc strip while the blue color of the solution fades, visible proof that Cu2+ ions are being consumed as zinc atoms are.

Every redox reaction, no matter how complicated, is really two simpler stories happening at once: one species losing electrons, another gaining exactly that many. Chemists exploit that structure directly by splitting a redox reaction into two separate half reactions, one for the oxidation and one for the reduction, which is exactly the tool introduced next.
